guide_description: Three days following Osaka's own north-to-south divide. Day one runs from the castle west along the river islands into Kita, the corporate and department store half of the city. Day two stays entirely in Minami, where the food and the neon are. Day three covers the older southern wards, from Japan's first state Buddhist temple to a 1912 tower and the tallest building in the country. Osaka rewards eating your way through a day rather than scheduling around meals.

days.cluster_name: The Castle, the River Islands and Kita
days.cluster_tagline: Hideyoshi's fortress, a civic island of brick and rose gardens, and a floating observatory at sunset
days.neighborhood_description: The castle sits in a large park on the eastern side of the centre, surrounded by moats wide enough to read as a small lake. West of it the Dojima and Tosabori rivers split around Nakanoshima, a long thin island holding the city's Taisho-era civic architecture, the main library, and a rose garden. Further north again is Umeda, the Kita business district, where three railway terminals and a dense stack of department stores sit on top of one another.

morning.notes: The keep is a 1931 concrete reconstruction with an elevator and a museum inside, so the honest pleasure here is the grounds: the cyclopean stones of the Otemon approach, some weighing over a hundred tonnes and hauled from Setouchi islands, and the scale of the moat system Hideyoshi ordered in 1583. Enter from Tanimachi 4-chome station and leave via Osakajokoen for the best sequence. Nishinomaru Garden holds roughly 600 cherry trees and charges separate admission during the early April bloom, when it is one of the two or three best hanami sites in Kansai. Confirm keep hours and last admission on the castle's official site before building the morning around going inside.

afternoon.notes: A three-kilometre sandbar between two rivers that functions as Osaka's civic spine. The Central Public Hall of 1918 is the landmark, red brick and Beaux-Arts, and the Prefectural Nakanoshima Library next door is older still and open to walk into. The rose garden at the eastern end peaks in May and again in October. If the weather turns, the Nakanoshima Museum of Art and the Museum of Oriental Ceramics are both on the island and both indoor alternatives that hold up for a full afternoon.

evening.notes: Two towers joined at the fortieth floor by a doughnut-shaped Floating Garden Observatory, reached by an escalator suspended across open air that is more memorable than the view itself. Aim to be up around forty minutes before sunset; the rooftop deck is open to the sky and windy, and the western view runs out over Osaka Bay. Tickets are timed and sell out on clear weekend evenings, so book online the day before. In the basement, Takimikoji is a reconstructed Showa-era alley of small restaurants, which is a better dinner than the tower floors above it.

if_time_permits.notes: Ten floors worked downward through time, starting with a full-scale reconstruction of the seventh-century Naniwa Palace hall on the top floor and ending with the Showa city. The building sits directly on the excavated palace foundations, visible in the basement, and the upper-floor windows give the best photograph of the castle keep across the moat. A reliable rainy-morning substitute for the castle grounds.

Dedicated to Sugawara no Michizane, the patron of scholarship, which fills the grounds with exam-season prayer plaques every winter. The shrine hosts Tenjin Matsuri on 24 and 25 July, one of the three great festivals of Japan, with a procession of boats on the Okawa and fireworks over the water. Tenjinbashisuji immediately north is the longest covered shopping street in Japan at 2.6 kilometres, and a good place to eat cheaply among locals.

days.cluster_tagline: A century-old market at breakfast, arcades in the afternoon, and the canal in full neon after dark
days.neighborhood_description: Minami is the southern half of central Osaka and the half people picture. Kuromon Ichiba supplies its restaurants, Shinsaibashi-suji runs six covered blocks of shopping north from the canal, Amerikamura holds the vintage and skate scene, and Dotonbori itself is a few hundred metres of canal frontage carrying more signage per square metre than anywhere in Japan. Everything here is within a fifteen-minute walk of everything else.

morning.notes: Six hundred metres of covered market that has fed Osaka's kitchens since the early nineteenth century and is known locally as the city's kitchen. Come at 9:00 when the fish stalls are still working rather than performing: uni, otoro, grilled scallops, and fugu in winter, most of it grilled to order and eaten standing at the stall. Prices have risen sharply as the market has shifted toward visitors, and the stalls a block off the main run are cheaper and better. Many close by mid-afternoon and Sunday trading is limited.

afternoon.notes: Shinsaibashi-suji is a covered arcade running roughly 600 metres north from the Dotonbori canal, which makes it the default plan in rain or in the August heat. Two blocks west, Amerikamura is the counterweight: vintage clothing, record shops, secondhand streetwear, and a small triangular park that has been the teenage gathering point since the 1970s. Midosuji, the boulevard between them, is lined with ginkgo trees that turn in mid-November and are lit through the winter. Cross to the Hozenji side for a coffee break when the arcades get to be too much.

evening.notes: The canal was cut in 1615 and the street became Osaka's theatre district long before it became its neon one. The Glico running man sign has been in place since 1935 in successive versions, and the standard photograph is taken from Ebisubashi, which will be shoulder to shoulder. Eat as you walk: takoyaki, kushikatsu with the strictly enforced no-double-dipping rule at the communal sauce tin, okonomiyaki in the Osaka style with everything mixed into the batter. The narrow lanes north of the canal, particularly Hozenji Yokocho, are where the food gets serious and the crowds thin.

if_time_permits.notes: A tiny temple in a flagstone alley one block from the loudest street in Osaka, and the contrast is the whole point. The Fudo Myoo statue is covered head to foot in moss, thickened by generations of visitors ladling water over it for luck. Come after dark when the lanterns are lit and the alley smells of the restaurants on either side. Two minutes off Dotonbori and consistently missed.

The main hall is an ordinary shrine building; the reason to come is the twelve-metre lion's head stage facing it, jaws open, built in 1974 and said to swallow bad luck. It is one of the strangest structures in the city and takes ten minutes to see. Free, rarely busy, and a short walk from Namba station, which makes it easy to fold into the start or end of the day.

days.cluster_tagline: Japan's oldest state temple, a 1912 tower over a fried-skewer district, and the country's tallest roof
days.neighborhood_description: South Osaka is older and rougher-edged than the centre and considerably cheaper. Shitenno-ji was founded in 593 and predates the city around it. Shinsekai was laid out in 1912 as a world's fair district modelled half on Paris and half on Coney Island, went into long decline, and now trades on that history with a wall of kushikatsu shops. Immediately south, Abeno Harukas rises 300 metres over Tennoji station, which is the sharpest juxtaposition Osaka offers.

morning.notes: Founded by Prince Shotoku in 593 and generally counted as the first Buddhist temple built by the Japanese state. The buildings are twentieth-century reconstructions after wartime bombing, faithful to the original south-facing axis of gate, pagoda and golden pavilion that gives the Shitennoji layout its name in Japanese architectural history. The outer grounds are free; the inner precinct, the treasure house and the Gokuraku-jodo garden are ticketed separately. A flea market fills the grounds on the 21st and 22nd of each month and is worth timing a visit around.

afternoon.notes: The current Tsutenkaku dates from 1956, replacing a 1912 original that was dismantled for scrap during the war, and the lighting on its upper section still functions as the neighbourhood's weather forecast. This is the home of kushikatsu, deep-fried skewers dipped once into a shared sauce tin, and Daruma is the chain that claims the invention. The district carries a slightly rough reputation that is mostly historical, though Shin-Imamiya immediately west remains a very different part of the city. Lunch here, since the portions and prices are the friendliest of the three days.

evening.notes: At 300 metres this has been the tallest building in Japan since it opened in 2014, sitting directly on top of Tennoji station. The Harukas 300 observatory occupies the top three floors around a full-height atrium, with a glass-floored edge walk on the outer deck. Go up about an hour before sunset and stay for the switch to night, when the whole southern half of the city lights up beneath you and Osaka Bay goes dark to the west. Book timed tickets in advance for clear evenings, and note the observatory ticket is separate from the department store and art museum in the same building.

if_time_permits.notes: The head shrine of some 2,300 Sumiyoshi shrines and one of the oldest architectural styles in Japan, sumiyoshi-zukuri, predating Chinese influence entirely. Four main halls stand in a formation said to represent a fleet at sea, and the steeply arched Sorihashi bridge over the pond is the image everyone takes away. Reached in about fifteen minutes from Tennoji on the Hankai tram, the last surviving streetcar line in Osaka and half the reason to go. Millions come for the first shrine visit of the New Year, when it is impassable.

The lawn at the northern entrance is free, open, and full of families, with Abeno Harukas rising directly behind it for the postcard shot. Keitakuen, tucked into the eastern corner, is a small circular-walk garden laid out for a Sumitomo family residence in the 1910s and charges a token admission that keeps it quiet. The Osaka Municipal Museum of Art sits between the two and is worth an hour if the weather turns.
